name: totonaco de Tuxtla / TOTU, 'totonaco de la Sierra'
confidence_why: Juárez Esteban 2026 (Tuxtla) and Troiani 1988 (Huehuetla) independently describe contrastive stress on the penultimate or final syllable that is unpredictable on roots, and the only note against it is Aschmann's 1983 [1962] popular dictionary remark that stress varies from village to village, which is not a competing analysis.

catalog_quote: Nótese que, en esta línea, se marca el acento léxico en la sílaba tónica con la tilde (´).5 [...] 5 El acento léxico en el TOTU cae usualmente en la penúltima o última sílaba y es fonológicamente contrastivo en algunos contextos (como en algunas distinciones aspectuales). Por esta razón, se representa el acento. [...] [printed p.56:] El singular no se marca y el plural se marca con dos formas: el prefijo lak- (con alomorfos laj-, laq-) y el sufijo -nin/-n/-Vn/-nV’. Los alomorfos -nin/-n/-Vn/-nV’ dependen de la fonología: -nin se usa cuando la base termina en sílaba tónica (CV́) (p.e. paatsapsná’ ‘albañil’, paatsapsna-nín ‘albañiles’); se usa -n con un tema que termina en vocal (p.e. skúni’ ‘trabajador’, skuní-n ‘trabajadores’); -Vn y -nV’ (V=vocal) se usa con un tema que termina en consonante (p.e. píxkalh ‘fiscal de la iglesia’, pixkálh-na’ ‘fiscales’).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Nótese que, en esta línea, se marca el acento léxico en la sílaba tónica con la tilde (´).5 [...] 5 El acento léxico en el TOTU cae usualmente en la penúltima o última sílaba y es fonológicamente contrastivo en algunos contextos (como en algunas distinciones aspectuales). Por esta razón, se representa el acento. [...] (p.55) Los alomorfos -nin/-n/-Vn/-nV’ dependen de la fonología: -nin se usa cuando la base termina en sílaba tónica (CV́) (p.e. paatsapsná’ ‘albañil’, paatsapsna-nín ‘albañiles’); se usa -n con un tema que termina en vocal (p.e. skúni’ ‘trabajador’, skuní-n ‘trabajadores’)
new_statements.translation: Note that, in this line, lexical stress is marked on the tonic syllable with the acute (´). [fn.5] Lexical stress in TOTU [Tuxtla Totonac] usually falls on the penultimate or the final syllable and is phonologically contrastive in some contexts (as in some aspectual distinctions). For this reason, stress is written. [...] (p.55) The allomorphs -nin/-n/-Vn/-nV’ depend on the phonology: -nin is used when the base ends in a stressed syllable (CV́) (e.g. paatsapsná’ ‘mason’, paatsapsna-nín ‘masons’); -n is used with a stem ending in a vowel (e.g. skúni’ ‘worker’, skuní-n ‘workers’).

Tesis de doctorado en Lingüística Indoamericana, Centro de Investigaciones y Estudios Superiores en Antropología Social (CIESAS), Ciudad de México. http://ciesas.repositorioinstitucional.mx/jspui/handle/1015/1932

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (482 pp., text layer present; alongside). At PDF p.32 = printed p.16, §1.3, the running text reads 'Nótese que, en esta línea, se marca el acento léxico en la sílaba tónica con la tilde (´).5' and footnote 5 reads exactly 'El acento léxico en el TOTU cae usualmente en la penúltima o última sílaba y es fonológicamente contrastivo en algunos contextos (como en algunas distinciones aspectuales). Por esta razón, se representa el acento.' The p.55 plural-allomorphy passage ('-nin se usa cuando la base termina en sílaba tónica (CV́) (p.e. paatsapsná’ ‘albañil’, paatsapsna-nín ‘albañiles’); se usa -n con un tema que termina en vocal (p.e. skúni’ ‘trabajador’, skuní-n ‘trabajadores’)')…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word (lexical) stress is confined to the last two syllables — usually penult or final — and is not fully predictable: the author marks it on every word and says it can be contrastive, e.g. distinguishing some aspect forms. Her marked forms pattern like other Totonac varieties (final stress on words ending in a consonant/glottal or long vowel: kintsé’, mintsumát, paatsapsná’; penult on light open finals: Klajkatsáni, skúni’), but no weight rule is stated in the source.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress said to be contrastive 'in some contexts (como en algunas distinciones aspectuales)'; stress/syllable shape conditions allomorphy (2sg -t after a closed final syllable or monosyllable, p.36; plural -nin after a stem-final stressed syllable, p.55). Enclitics such as =i (juncture) are written attached but appear to fall outside the stress domain (Klajkatsán=i). Note the older first-hand note for the same municipality, Aschmann 1962/1983 p.142, claims stress 'es muy variable y cambia de pueblo en pueblo' and can be shifted without changing meaning — a popular orthographic remark that contradicts the modern statement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('acento léxico'), marked on running-text examples from a spoken corpus, so forms are in phrasal context rather than citation forms; the thesis has no phonology chapter and states the variant's phonology is undescribed. Variety = Tuxtla, municipio Zapotitlán de Méndez (same municipality as Aschmann's reference dialect of Highland/Sierra Totonac).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Tuxtla Totonac (community of Tuxtla, municipio Zapotitlán de Méndez, Puebla; 'TOTU', self-classified as totonaco de la Sierra), i.e. the same municipality as Aschmann's Zapotitlán de Méndez reference dialect of Highland Totonac [tos, high1243]. Supporting first-hand material comes from Zapotitlán de Méndez itself (Aschmann 1946, 1962/1983) and from Olintla (Tino Antonio 2020), which Glottolog also files under high1243. Coatepec (McQuown, Levy) and Huehuetla/Ozelonacaxtla (Troiani, Román Lobato) are further Highland varieties whose descriptions were not accessible. Not to be confused with Reid 1991 (Xicotepec, xico1235) or Beck's Upper Necaxa (uppe1275).

new_statements.quote: L'accent est un accent d'intensité et de hauteur accompagné parfois d'un léger allongement vocalique. [...] Il est fonctionnel puisqu'il permet des oppositions 'čiči "chaud" / či'či "chien" [...] Toute racine lexémique porte un accent qui n'est pas prévisible [...] – la préfixation morphématique n'en modifie pas la place ; – par contre, en cas de suffixation, l'accent se déplace sur la droite selon la règle suivante : l'accent tombe sur l'avant dernière syllabe sauf quand le mot se termine par une sonante /m/, /n/, /y/, /l/, /w/ auquel cas il se place sur la dernière syllabe. Ces quelques règles ne concernent que le verbe
new_statements.translation: The accent is an accent of intensity and pitch, sometimes accompanied by slight vowel lengthening. [...] It is functional, since it permits oppositions: 'čiči 'hot' / či'či 'dog' [...] Every lexical root carries an accent which is not predictable [...] – morphological prefixation does not change its position; – on the other hand, under suffixation the accent moves to the right by the following rule: the accent falls on the penultimate syllable except when the word ends in a sonorant /m/, /n/, /y/, /l/, /w/, in which case it goes on the last syllable. These few rules concern only the verb
new_statements.citation: Troiani, Duna (1988). De la prédication en totonaque, commune de Huehuetla, Puebla, Mexique. Université de Paris IV. 295 pp.
new_statements.locator: §2.3 L'ACCENT, printed pp.59–60 (PDF pp.64–65); also p.62 fn.1 (notation), p.92 (accent-bearing prefix aq-), p.109 (possessive-pronoun plurals)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: sous la direction de B. Pottier, 297 p.'). Section '2.3. L'ACCENT' is on PDF p.64 (printed page number 59 at the foot) and continues on PDF p.65 (printed 60): points 1-5 read exactly as quoted: '1. L'accent est un accent d'intensité et de hauteur accompagné parfois d'un léger allongement vocalique. 2. Il est fonctionnel puisqu'il permet des oppositions 'čiči "chaud" / či'či "chien"; 'kuku "oncle" / ku'ku "sable". 3. Toute racine lexémique porte un accent qui n'est pas prévisible; nous avons choisi de le noter même sur les racines monosyllabiques. (Il existe des morphèmes monosyllabiques clitiques.) 4.. – toute racine lexémique porte un accent; – la préfixation morphématique n'en modifie pas…
new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the catalog's existing Tuxtla statement (Juárez Esteban 2026: stress usually penultimate or final, phonologically contrastive in some contexts; read 'lexical (unpredictable)'), and adds the conditioning: root accent unpredictable and contrastive; in suffixed (verbal) words penultimate unless the word ends in a sonorant consonant, then final; prefixes inert; secondary accent on grammaticalised body-part prefixes. Different locality (Huehuetla vs Tuxtla) but no disagreement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (intensity + pitch, sometimes slight lengthening) is contrastive and its position on a bare lexical root is not predictable ('čiči 'hot' vs či'či 'dog'; 'kuku 'uncle' vs ku'ku 'sand'). Prefixes leave it in place; when suffixes are added the accent shifts rightward to the penultimate syllable, or to the final syllable if the word ends in a sonorant (m, n, y, l, w). The author states the suffixation rule for verbs only and leaves nominal derivation/composition unverified. Stress marked with ' before the stressed syllable throughout the thesis (p.62 fn.1).
new_statements.secondary_stress: §2.3 point 5 (p.60): 'morphèmes accentogènes' — grammaticalised body-part lexemes such as the prefix aq- 'head' carry an 'accent second' (secondary accent), which is why their vowel does not delete in some morphological constructions (e.g. ki-aq-'kaw 'I am ten years old', p.92).
new_statements.exceptions: Accent can move under derivation ('čankat → kačan'katni 'sugar-cane field', §3.2.6) and verbal morphosyntax; rules given only for the verb, nominal composition/derivation to be checked; monosyllabic clitics are unaccented; determiner wa loses the accent that the pronoun 'wa keeps (p.101 area); possessive pronouns with plural marks shift the accent to the last syllable: ki-'la-kan → kila'kan, kilaka'nin (p.109).
new_statements.identity_note: Troiani 1988 describes the Totonac of the municipio of Huehuetla, Puebla (fieldwork at Chilocoyo/Huehuetla, Sierra Norte de Puebla), one of the Highland/Sierra localities grouped under high1243 in this reading; the catalog's existing statement is from Tuxtla (municipio Zapotitlán de Méndez). Levy 2015, unopened, is about Coatepec Totonac as recorded by McQuown in 1938–1940.

new_statements.quote: el acento gráfico se predice por criterios métricos: aparece en la última sílaba de la secuencia a menos que la vocal final de la secuencia fuera breve, ante pausa (en los textos), en cuyo caso el acento salta a la penúltima sílaba. [...] sílabas que terminan en vocal larga o que están trabadas por cualquier consonante, cuentan como pesadas y llevan el acento. Esta regla corresponde a la que da McQuown en su Gramática (§ 5.1) como regla de acentuación de palabra. La regla se cumple sin excepciones a lo largo de todo el corpus textual. [...] no hay excepciones salvo los préstamos del español.
new_statements.translation: the written accent is predicted by metrical criteria: it appears on the last syllable of the sequence unless the final vowel of the sequence is short, before pause (in the texts), in which case the accent jumps to the penultimate syllable. [...] syllables that end in a long vowel or that are closed by any consonant count as heavy and carry the accent. This rule corresponds to the one McQuown gives in his Gramática (§5.1) as the word-accentuation rule. The rule holds without exception throughout the whole text corpus. [...] there are no exceptions apart from the loans from Spanish.
new_statements.citation: Levy, Paulette. 2015. La fonología prosódica del totonaco de Coatepec: los textos totonacos de N. A. McQuown (1938–1940). Memorias del VII Congreso de Idiomas Indígenas de Latinoamérica (CILLA VII), 29–31 de octubre de 2015. Austin: University of Texas at Austin / AILLA.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for high1243 has an empty rule; the one existing statement (Juárez Esteban 2026, Tuxtla Totonac) reads stress as lexical: 'usualmente en la penúltima o última sílaba y es fonológicamente contrastivo en algunos contextos'. Levy 2015 gives, for the Coatepec variety (coat1246, a dialect listed under high1243), a fully predictable weight-sensitive final/penult rule with no lexical exceptions other than Spanish loans, and even questions whether there is word-level accent distinct from phrasal accent. Same final-or-penult window, but a different type (predictable by weight vs. lexically contrastive). The difference may be dialectal (Coatepec vs Tuxtla) rather than a factual dis…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Coatepec Totonac (McQuown's 1938-40 texts and Gramática §5.1) accent is fully predictable from the weight of the final syllable of the accentual domain: final if the last syllable is heavy (long vowel, or closed by any consonant), penultimate if it ends in a short (devoiced) vowel. McQuown states it as the word-accent rule; Levy finds it exceptionless over the corpus, the conjugations and the lexical index. Each string McQuown writes between blanks carries exactly one accent, which Levy analyses as a phonological-phrase accent; since word accent and phrasal accent obey the same rule she notes it cannot be decided from words in isolation whether the language has a separate word accent at all ('O bien, que en este totonaco no haya acento de palabra.. Quedan por investigarse cuáles serían los criterios para determinar el acento de palabra', PDF p.9).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress; only one accent per phonological phrase is marked. Certain monosyllables (e.g. tuu 'lo.que', páks) are tonic in some contexts and proclitic/atonic in others (§2, PDF p.6; fn.10).
new_statements.exceptions: Only Spanish loanwords: the Spanish stressed final vowel is reinterpreted as long and therefore takes final accent (pa:lí 'padre', puːyú 'pollo', fn.8 PDF p.11). Underlying vowel length of the final vowel surfaces only utterance-finally (before pause); phrase-finally inside an utterance a final vowel is always lengthened (R3) and so takes the accent there.
new_statements.identity_note: Levy 2015 describes Coatepec Totonac (totonaco de Coatepec, Sierra Norte de Puebla; Glottolog coat1246, listed as a dialect of high1243), nearly extinct, as recorded by N. A. McQuown in 1938-40 (texts written by Manuel Oropeza Castro, recordings 1950, and McQuown's Gramática). The catalog item name refers to Tuxtla (Zapotitlán de Méndez); the existing statement is for Tuxtla.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the sources opened. Troiani 1988 (Huehuetla) and the catalog's Juárez Esteban 2026 statement (Tuxtla) both give contrastive lexical stress that falls on the penultimate or final syllable; Troiani adds the sonorant-final condition for final stress in suffixed verbs and notes that root accent is unpredictable. The only tension already on record is Aschmann's popular dictionary note (Zapotitlán) that stress is 'muy variable y cambia de pueblo en pueblo', which is a caution about cross-village variation rather than a competing rule. Levy 2015 (Coatepec, McQuown's 1938–40 texts) could not be opened, so its position is unknown. Within glottocode high1243 the sources describe different local varieties and do not agree on the type of accent: Levy 2015 (Coatepec, from McQuown 1938-40, = McQuown Gramática §5.1) states an exceptionless weight-sensitive rule (final syllable if heavy, i.e. long vowel or closed; otherwise penult; Spanish loans the only exceptions) and raises the possibility that the accent is phrasal rather than word-level; Juárez Esteban 2026 (Tuxtla, the existing catalog statement) says accent is usually penult or final and phonologically contrastive in some contexts (lexical); Troiani 1988 (Huehuetla, already) gives unpredictable root accent with rightward shift under suffixation (penult unless the word ends in a sonorant, then final); Aschmann 1962/1983 (Zapotitlán) says accent varies from town to town. All agree on a final/penult window; they di…
